item.title: SA installer flagged by regulator crackdown gets five months in the sin bin
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: A South Australian installer has been identified by the Clean Energy Regulator's three-strikes rule crackdown on solar retailers and installers who demonstrate poor workmanship, declaring him ineligible to install systems for five months.
item.content:encoded:
The Clean Energy Regulator (CER) has reiterated its call on solar retailers and installers to ‘do it once and do it well’ as it progresses a a three-strikes rule crackdown on poor workmanship, and most recently has flagged a South Australian (SA) accredited installer.

Under the directive, the CER declares David Mogg ineligible for five months to install solar or battery systems under the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme (SRES) or to receive small-scale technology certificates (STCs).

Inspections of Mogg’s work identified aspects of an installation that did not meet Australian standards or scheme requirements, the CER said.

CER Chair Tony Chappel said the organisation has been warning installers it won’t hesitate to act when unsafe and non-compliant work is identified.

“Our inspection reports and letters clearly set out what needs to improve and warn that further compliance action may follow,” Chappel said.

“If that advice is not taken seriously and issues continue, we will act.”

Under Regulation 47 of the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Regulations 2001, the CER may declare a person ineligible to participate in the SRES if they are subject to an adverse finding in an inspection report on three separate occasions.

Action under the regulation operates separately, and in addition to, any compliance actions that can be taken by accreditation bodies or states and territories.

A CER statement said its approach is to support installers in complying with their obligations, while taking firmer action when ongoing non-compliance is identified.

Since 1 July 2025, the CER has communicated with over 830 installers regarding adverse inspection outcomes and their obligations under the scheme.

This includes 718 initial advisory letters to installers for first-time non-compliance, and 121 warning letters to installers with repeated non-compliance. 

“The message to installers continues to be, to do it once and do it well,” Chappel said.

“Poor and unsafe work will be found out, and installers will be required to return to site and rectify any issues or face the consequences.”

item.title: EcoFlow expands Ocean 2 range with new 8 kWh home battery
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: EcoFlow has introduced a new product to its Ocean 2 residential energy range, with an 8 kWh battery delivering up to 32 kWh capacity to help meet demand, where 1 GWh of small-scale battery energy storage was installed in Australia just October 2026.
item.content:encoded:
China-headquartered clean energy company EcoFlow has expanded it’s home energy portfolio in Australia with the introduction of the Ocean 2, 8 kWh residential battery offering a higher-capacity storage solution that deliveres more storage within each module, reducing the number required for larger installations.

Ocean 2 supports up to three wall-mounted 8 kWh batteries, delivering 24 kWh of storage capacity, or four floor-mounted offering up to 32 kWh capacity.

The system supports configurations from 5 kWh to 96 kWh per inverter, weighs 67.5kg per battery and comes with a standard ten-year warranty, with an optional paid five-year extension available through participating installers.

EcoFlow Head of Residential UK & ANZ Craig Bilboe said Australia is already leading the way in rooftop solar, but generating electricity is only part of the picture.

“The next step is helping households store and use more of that energy effectively. Our new 8 kWh battery makes it easier for installers to deliver higher-capacity storage without adding unnecessary complexity,” Bilboe said.

“With fewer modules, flexible configurations and intelligent energy management, we’re helping make home energy storage more practical for Australian households.”

The new 8 kWh battery joins EcoFlow’s OCEAN 2 residential energy portfolio, including OCEAN 2 Three-Phase and OCEAN 2 Plus Single-Phase solutions.

Energy management systems

The solution is supported by energy management systems, including the remote monitoring system, the EcoFlow App and the in-home 11-inch PowerInsight 2 home energy monitor.

The EcoFlow app brings solar generation, battery storage and household electricity consumption together in one interface, and transforms complex energy data into clear, accessible insights, allowing homeowners to monitor system performance and understand how their electricity is being used.

The PowerInsight 2 provides a dedicated touchscreen in-home display showing how much solar energy is being generated, tracking battery levels and monitoring household consumption.

Australia’s installation of residential battery systems has exceeded 600,000, with a recent report from SunWiz showing Australian households and businesses installed an estimated 1,043 MWh of battery energy storage (5-100 kWh) capacity in October 2026, up 18% more than the 885 MWh registered in the same month in 2025, up 9.7% on the 966.5 MWh registered in September 2026, and the strongest month since April 2026’s 3,262 MWh peak.

item.title: Hybrid monofacial-bifacial PV arrays boost power output under shading
item.dc:creator: Lior Kahana
item.description: Researchers tested a nine-module array combining six monofacial and three bifacial panels under 12 illumination patterns. The experiments assessed how module placement and electrical reconfiguration influence power output.
item.content:encoded:
A research team in India has experimentally investigated the performance of a photovoltaic array combining monofacial and bifacial solar modules.

“To mitigate power increase and cost, a hybrid PV array arrangement incorporates a small number of bifacial modules within a traditional monofacial array,” the researchers said.

“Employing a switching matrix-based reconfiguration approach, the most effective hybrid configuration was dynamically selected.”

The researchers tested different configurations of a 3 × 3 PV array to determine how to increase power output while limiting costs.

They assembled a 3 × 3 PV array with nine modules electrically connected in a total-cross-tied configuration. They first measured the voltage, current, and power output of a reference array comprising nine 10 W monofacial modules. They then replaced three of the modules with 12 W bifacial modules to create a hybrid array.

The team tested six configurations, placing the three bifacial modules in different positions: diagonally in the top-left, center, and bottom-right positions; across the top row; down the leftmost column; in the center and the two bottom corners; in the top-right and two bottom corners; and in the top-middle, top-right, and bottom-right positions. The remaining six positions in each configuration were occupied by monofacial modules.

The researchers conducted rooftop experiments at Kamaraj College of Engineering and Technology in southern India under 12 irradiance conditions: no shading, uneven column shading, uneven row shading, diagonal shading, plus-shaped shading, center shading, corner shading, outer shading, short-and-wide shading, long-and-wide shading, left-corner shading, and random shading.

They compared the electrical performance of each hybrid configuration with that of the all-monofacial reference array. They also investigated whether switching between different configurations could improve power output under changing shading conditions.

In the “double-hybrid” analysis, the researchers compared pairs of configurations, while the “triple-hybrid” analysis considered groups of three. For each shading pattern, they selected the configuration delivering the highest power output within each pair or group.

“In the double-hybrid analysis, bifacial placements in the first column and grouped configurations ((2 × 2), (3 × 1), and (3 × 3)) consistently delivered superior performance, with power output ranging from 95 W under no-shading conditions to 26 W under severe shading, outperforming other configurations in nine shading scenarios,” the researchers said.

“Similarly, the triple-hybrid comparison showed that first-row and first-column placements, along with grouped configurations, achieved maximum power in a greater number of shading cases.”

The researchers presented their findings in “An experimental investigation of photovoltaic array with mixed mono-facial and bi-facial modules,” published in Scientific Reports. The research team included scientists from India’s M. Kumarasamy College of Engineering, Kamaraj College of Engineering and Technology, Sri Vidya College of Engineering & Technology, Vardhaman College of Engineering, and Chitkara University.

From pv magazine Global

item.title: New Zealand confirms 2028 rollout for battery market reforms
item.dc:creator: Brian Publicover
item.description: Battery owners in New Zealand will be able to trade their full capacity and submit offers with up to 10 price bands, compared with five for other generators, from March 2028, while consultation on rules for battery-hybrid plants has slipped into next year, according to the country’s electricity regulator.
item.content:encoded:
New Zealand’s electricity market regulator, the Electricity Authority Te Mana Hiko, said it has corrected the effective date of a battery market rule to March 31, 2028, and moved consultation on market arrangements for battery-hybrid plants to early 2027.

The corrected rule allows battery owners to submit offers with up to 10 price bands. Its effective date was wrong in both the decision paper and the amendment to the Electricity Industry Participation Code the regulator published in September.

The consultation on wholesale market and common quality arrangements for battery-hybrid stations had been planned for late 2026. The authority said it will shortly issue guidance on how prospective hybrid plant owners can operate and trade in the market in the interim.

The rules, set out in a Sept. 29 decision, are being introduced in two phases because the required software upgrades will take time. Since Oct. 30, utility-scale batteries have had to be dispatchable when charging from the grid, not just when discharging.

“We consider they should be dispatchable across their full operational range as they are highly controllable assets,” the authority said in its decision paper.

As an interim measure, battery owners can trade on their expected capability and update offer and bid quantities after gate closure, the point at which bids and offers must be locked in before dispatch, if that capability changes.

The regulator said the existing arrangements may lead to conservative trading, because a battery’s ability to charge or discharge can change quickly as its stored energy changes.

Full capacity

From March 31, 2028, battery owners will be able to trade their full capacity, with state-of-charge constraints in the dispatch software limiting charging and discharging to feasible levels based on stored energy.

They will submit charging bids and discharging offers on a single trade form and receive a single dispatch instruction. They will also have 10 price bands each for bids and offers, compared with a maximum of five for offers from other generators.

Gate closure for offers from batteries connected to local distribution networks will move from 30 minutes to one hour, aligning them with batteries connected directly to the transmission grid. The authority deferred the change after industry feedback and pushed the final phase back three months to upgrade the System Operator’s software for multiple frequency keeping, an ancillary service that maintains grid frequency.

The September decision paper said four utility-scale batteries were connected to New Zealand’s power system, with many more planned.

New Zealand’s grid-scale battery fleet has grown as its hydro-dominated power system faces climate pressures. Contact Energy opened its Glenbrook battery south of Auckland in June, and French manufacturer Saft was selected to supply a 200 MWh battery project in the country in 2024.

From ESS News

item.title: Edify seeks federal tick for Queensland solar and battery project
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Australian renewable energy and storage developer Edify Energy has unveiled plans to build an 800 MW solar farm and an 800 MW / 3,200 MWh battery energy storage system in southwest Queensland.
item.content:encoded:
Edify Energy’s Glenarbon Solar Power Station project planned for Queensland’s Darling Downs region has entered the pipeline of projects seeking approval under the federal government’s Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation (EPBC) Act.

The Glenarbon project, planned for a 1,500-hectare site about 65 kilometres east of Goondiwindi near the New South Wales border, combines an 800 MW solar farm with an 800 MW, four-hour capacity battery energy storage system (BESS).

According to documents referred for assessment under the federal EPBC Act, the facility would plug into the National Electricity Market (NEM) via an existing Powerlink 330 kV transmission line that crosses the project area.

Edify said once operational, the project could generate up to 1,555,000 MWh of dispatchable renewable energy per annum.

“The proposed BESS component will store excess energy generated by the solar farm and support the grid by providing power to the grid in peak periods of demand or when there is a lack of energy generation,” the developer said.

The proposed site has been largely cleared and is currently being used for grazing sheep and cattle. Ultimately, Edify expects the project will not be considered a controlled action as any potential negative impacts will be minimised through implementation of mitigation measures.

The project is part of Edify’s expanding portfolio of renewable energy generation and storage projects.

Now owned by Canadian investment group La Caisse, Edify was one of the early movers in the battery market in Australia, building the country’s first co-located battery at Gannawarra – adjacent to but separately connected to a solar farm.

It now has 17 solar projects and 16 batteries, either standalone or backing up PV, in its portfolio, including the Smoky Creek and Guthrie’s Gap, and Ganymirra and Majors Creek projects Queensland, which in aggregate supply 1,080 MWp of solar together with 900 MW / 3,600 MWh of DC-coupled battery energy storage.

Edify has also received environmental approval from the federal government for its Nowingi Solar Power Station project planned for northwest Victoria. It will combine a 300 MW solar plant with a 300 MW / 2,400 MWh BESS.

item.title: Transmission lines emerge as election flashpoint in Victoria
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Electricity transmission lines are a hot-button issue in the upcoming Victorian election. Following farm-gate blockades and protests outside the Victorian parliament, both the Coalition and One Nation have promised to scrap a multi-billion-dollar project in the state's northwest.
item.content:encoded:
If the polls are correct and Victoria changes government, what would this mean for energy policy and regional Australia?

For the past century, coal-fired power plants have supplied most of Victoria’s electricity. But some plants have already retired and the rest will follow. The capacity they provide urgently needs replacing. Renewables produced about 44% of Victoria’s electricity last year.

To shift to a system largely powered by renewables, Victoria will need new high-voltage lines. These are meant to deliver energy from new rural solar and wind farms to cities and industrial centres, as well as stabilising the grid by making it easier to trade electricity between states.

New transmission lines are a key component of state and federal efforts to overhaul the National Electricity Market.

In Victoria, the two biggest projects in the works are the 190-kilometre Western Renewables Link (WRL) west of Melbourne, and the Victoria to New South Wales (NSW)Interconnector (VNI) West, spanning around 240 km in Victoria and a similar length in NSW. Both are well advanced through state planning processes, but neither has begun construction.

A recent survey showed the energy transition has majority support in regional Victoria. But opponents of the two lines are vocal and organised.

Where do the parties stand?

Vocal opponents of transmission projects are running as regional candidates for the Nationals and One Nation.

Earlier in the election campaign, the Coalition promised to pause both projects pending a review of Victoria’s transmission plan. In August, it changed tack on VNI West, promising to cancel it if elected.

One Nation has gone further by pledging to scrap VNI West, WRL and other major transmission projects.

In September, Premier Ben Carroll ordered an immediate cost assessment of WRL, but his Labor government remains committed to building VNI West.

The Greens are supportive of new transmission lines to unlock renewables, but have criticised the government handling of WRL.

What’s driving this opposition?

Opponents cite a range of concerns, such as disruption to farming, visual impact, bushfire risk, threats to biodiversity and pressures on local services.

A common theme is that rural areas are being expected to do too much for the benefit of energy users in cities. “Our job is to feed the city not supply its electricity!” as one protest sign put it.

Most opposition doesn’t stem from a rejection of climate science, though this is a feature of One Nation’s policies. Experts have raised concerns about misinformation and disinformation amplifying opposition of transmission projects. This is a factor, but there are legitimate concerns in the mix.

One real point of contention is the power transmission network operators have to compulsorily acquire easements on private land, allowing them access to build and maintain power lines. This is quite different to solar or wind projects where landholders remain free to choose whether or not to host them.

The state government has offered benefit packages of $200,000 per kilometre to landholders hosting power lines on top of compensation payments. There are broader community benefit funds, too.

Some farmers are keen to host transmission towers, as the stable income stream can help them through leaner years. For others, the question is less about money and more about dissatisfaction with the consultation process and distrust of project backers.

Flashpoints for rural discontent

For some residents, the real issue is resisting the industrialisation of rural areas, as captured in one group’s slogan: “No to lines, mines and turbines!” Others are supportive of renewables, but critical of proposed transmission routes.

Recent research shows opposition to transmission lines is also a proxy for bigger debates about regional Australia’s intersecting challenges, from extreme weather and cost-of-living pressures to deteriorating roads and poor access to services.

The two council areas in Victoria with the highest proportion of roads in poor condition (Gannawarra and Buloke) are both in VNI West’s path.

Many rural residents feel their areas have been forgotten. Saying no to transmission lines sends a message that rural communities need to be heard.

Can transmission projects be done differently?

It remains to be seen whether VNI West or WRL will survive the state election. But the tensions on display in Victoria have clear lessons for future projects, as our research shows:

  1. Early, sustained and respectful community engagement is vital, not only on proposed transmission projects but on regional futures more broadly.
  2. People in regional Australia don’t view transmission projects in isolation, but as part of the broader effects of the clean energy transition and other stresses and uncertainties they face.
  3. Governments, businesses and communities need to work together at regional and local levels to manage these effects and harness cumulative benefits, such as jobs and investment in community facilities.
  4. Community benefit programs need to be designed with affected communities rather than imposed top-down. They must be delivered as part of broader commitments by government and business to promote prosperity and wellbeing in regional communities.

A people-powered energy transition

If Victoria’s transmission projects are scrapped without a credible alternative, the state will face the real risk of less reliable electricity.

It’s vital to keep the lights on while shifting to cheaper and cleaner sources of power. But that’s not the full picture.

Rural communities have a major stake in how Australia’s energy transition pans out. It’s only fair they have a say in figuring out how the benefits to regional Australia can outweigh the costs.

Authors: Jonathan Pickering, Associate Professor, Canberra School of Government, University of Canberra; Stephanie Rosestone, Community Fellow, University of Canberra; Australian National University; Wendy Conway-Lamb, Postdoctoral Research Fellow, Centre for Deliberative Democracy and Centre for Environmental Governance, University of Canberra

Jonathan Pickering receives funding from the Australian Research Council.

Stephanie Rosestone receives funding from the Australian Research Council. From 2020-21, Stephanie was involved in the Save Wattle Flat community group, which raised concerns about local impacts of the Western Renewables Link.

Wendy Conway-Lamb receives funding from the Australian Research Council.

This article was initially published in The Conversation and is republished here under a Creative Commons Licence.

item.title: Tesla unveils Powercore medium-voltage power electronics platform
item.dc:creator: Ben Zientara
item.description: By replacing traditional transformers with a consolidated solid-state platform, the company aims to bypass supply chain bottlenecks and accelerate project timelines across utility-scale solar, battery storage, and AI data centres.
item.content:encoded:
Tesla has announced the introduction of Powercore, a consolidated medium-voltage power electronics platform that combines a solid-state transformer, switchgear, and an inverter into a single enclosure rated for a nominal DC voltage of 800 V to 2,000 V and an AC voltage of 10 kV to 34.5 kV, providing up to 7.4 MW (9 MVA) of power at 34.5 kV AC.

Powercore will be manufactured at Tesla facilities in the United States and the company plans to have it in operation in 2027. The company said the platform is designed to operate from −40°C to 55°C and can be covered by a warranty of up to 25 years.

The Powercore platform is aimed at numerous segments in the modern energy ecosystem, specifically targeting solar, energy storage, data centre power and EV charging. Tesla said the Powercore offers unique benefits for each of these use cases, but the overarching advantage might be the ability to bypass the supply chain for conventional transformers. Limits to the availability of key inputs to transformer manufacturing has caused lead times of as long as four years, resulting in a bottleneck in grid modernisation and renewable energy deployment.

“We’ve done 3 TW of power converters at Tesla,” said AJ Booth, the company’s head of energy and charging, in an interview with pv magazine. “We build all of our power converters in-house, and we wanted to use that capability to provide a bankable and reliable pathway for customers to confidently adopt what is fundamentally a new technology to the industry.”

Bringing the manufacturing of critical power infrastructure in-house could also provide a catalyst to grow the company’s high-margin energy revenue, which represents roughly 10% of the company’s overall sales. Margins for the Energy Generation and Storage division have routinely outperformed those of the company’s core automotive business, despite experiencing some quarter-to-quarter volatility in revenue.

Streamlining utility-scale solar and storage deployments

For solar installations, Powercore accepts high-voltage direct current directly from solar arrays, combining the transformer, inverter and switchgear into a single product. The company said the hardware natively supports existing 1,500 V DC plants as well as emerging 2,000 V DC architectures. This eliminates the need for asset owners to purchase secondary inverters and transformers.

On the energy storage side, the platform is designed to integrate with Tesla Megapack batteries via DC bus connectors. The company said the two solutions can be delivered to a site pre-assembled, speeding up deployment and reducing manual on-site wiring. By simplifying site design and lowering labor costs, the integrated architecture can lead to improved project economics for developers while maintaining Tesla’s high equipment margins.

Advanced safety and grid-forming capabilities

Tesla said Powercore features the industry’s first built-in solid-state circuit breaker. The system can clear electrical faults in 100 microseconds — far faster than conventional transformer-fed protection.

“We think we’re safer because we can interrupt faults a thousand times faster than traditional equipment, which is extremely safe for personnel and for equipment due to our integrated solid-state circuit breaker design,” Booth said.

The platform also targets the power requirements of artificial intelligence computing. Tesla said Powercore is designed to sidestep the complicated method of stepping down grid voltage through multiple stages to power data centre racks by reducing the conversion to a single step that takes grid power from the feeder and outputs 800 V DC power to the servers.

The company said it is working with NVIDIA to certify Powercore into the DSX Ready Program, which validates equipment that meets standards for integration with next-generation data centres. As of September, Tesla’s Megapack 2XL was one of only three battery energy storage system (BESS) offerings qualified under the DSX Ready program.

When paired with Megapack battery storage on the grid, Powercore uses Tesla’s grid-forming controls to provide synthetic inertia and reactive power support. Booth stated that managing a data centre’s dynamic loads with this paired system can smooth local voltage oscillations and stabilise the broader grid network.

“By adding a data centre with Powercore and Megapack, we can provide a stiffer local grid and provide a more stable grid,” Booth said. “It’s actually better than if you didn’t put a data centre there at all, which is the amazing thing that batteries can do for the grid.”

Tesla is presenting the new Powercore product this week at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas.

From pv magazine USA

item.title: Helping homeowners understand practicalities of battery backup
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Home battery uptake continues to surge with more than 600,000 batteries installed across Australia in the past 18 months, but many consumers remain in the dark about energy storage system’s capabilities, including when it comes to backup, outages, and changeover switching.
item.content:encoded:
Australia’s growing fleet of small-scale batteries is changing the dynamics of electricity generation and demand but some confusion about just what individual energy storage systems provide for consumers remains.

One homeowner messaged us in August to ask whether the 42 kWh battery we had quoted came with blackout backup. When we said it did not, the next message was: “I thought having a larger battery installed would cover the entire house during a black out?”

It was a fair assumption. Battery offers are sold almost entirely on kWh, and backup is usually a separate line, or a footnote. We wanted to know how often our own enquiries started from the same place.

We went back through 192 Facebook Messenger conversations with South East Queensland homeowners from mid-June to early November 2026. We re-read every conversation that mentioned backup, blackouts, outages, whole-home supply or changeover switching. After removing supplier spam, off-grid enquiries and keyword false matches, 30 remained: 29 before a sale and one from an existing customer after installation. This is one installer’s enquiries, so the numbers show direction rather than market share. A conversation can also fall into more than one group.

The most common question was simply whether backup was in the price. Thirteen of the 30 asked it in some form. One said the system “should include blackout backup without extra fee.”

In Sunny Energy quotes, and in the one competitor quote a homeowner shared with us in detail, backup was a separate optional item, priced after an electrician had looked at the switchboard. So two quotes for “28 kWh installed” could describe two different jobs, and the homeowner had no easy way to tell.

Three people gave us a budget ceiling that included backup, for example a fixed figure “including blackout points X2”. That is a sensible way to buy, but it only works if every installer prices backup the same way.

Two groups, one word

The rest of the conversations fell into two groups that used the same words.

Nine people wanted a short list. Freezers, the internet, TV, or, lights, the fridge and the internet. “A minimum of one light and one power circuit.” For them, backing up two or three chosen circuits was the right answer.

Eight wanted the whole house, or assumed that was what backup meant. Six asked for it directly. One, quoted above, linked it to battery size. The eighth was an existing customer who contacted us after a power cut, surprised that only one room was getting battery power.

Capacity is not the limit people think it is

Battery capacity, in kWh, decides how long backup lasts. The inverter’s backup output, in kW, and the circuits wired to it decide what can run at the same time. Start-up current from air conditioners, pumps and ovens is often what trips the system first.

A 42kWh battery behind a backup output of a few kW can keep a fridge, lights and the NBN going for a long time. It will not run ducted air conditioning, an oven and a pool pump together. We had one request to back up air conditioning, a pool pump, a fridge and a stove at the same house. Another homeowner wanted every power point except the oven, air conditioning and EV charger. Neither request is unreasonable, but both need an answer in kW, not kWh.

Three people asked whether their solar would keep running in an outage. One said that was the main reason they wanted backup. The honest answer depends on the design. In many AC-coupled retrofits the existing solar inverter stays off during an outage unless the system is built to let it run. Panels connected to a hybrid inverter can usually keep charging the battery while the house is off the grid. For someone worried about a three-day outage after a storm, this matters more than another 10 kWh of storage.

What automatic switching looks like

Two homeowners asked whether changeover was automatic or needed a manual switch. Both answers exist, so it is a fair question.

Our installer recorded a short demonstration of a whole-home backup gateway at a switchboard. He turns the grid supply off, and within a few seconds the house is running on the battery. When he turns the grid back on, the gateway waits to confirm the supply is stable before switching back. He counts 13 seconds on camera. Counting from a slightly different point in the footage, it is closer to 18. The manufacturer quotes about 20.

Two practical points come out of that. Automatic changeover is not the same as an uninterruptible power supply, so a desktop computer or some modems may still restart. And the wait on the way back is deliberate. A homeowner who has been told the switchover is “seamless” may think something is wrong when the lights stay on battery for another 20 seconds.

Five things a backup quote should say

Whole-home gateways from several battery manufacturers now make whole-house backup a practical, separately priced option. That makes it more important, not less, for a quote to say which kind of backup is being sold. From these conversations, I think a quote that mentions blackout protection should state five things in writing before anyone signs:

  1. Whether backup is included, and if not, its price or a capped range.
  2. Whether it covers selected circuits or the whole home, with any selected circuits named in plain language, such as “kitchen power” or “upstairs lights”.
  3. The continuous backup output in kW, and which appliances should not run together during an outage.
  4. Whether changeover is automatic or manual, and roughly how long it takes in each direction.
  5. Whether the solar keeps generating and recharging the battery while the grid is down.

None of this needs new technology. It needs the backup scope to be decided, or at least capped, before the contract is signed, rather than discovered at handover. The homeowners in our sample were already asking these questions.

Author: Richard Liu, owner, SUNNY Energy

item.title: Sungrow launches C&I storage solution with modular scenario dock and full SiC PCS
item.dc:creator: Vincent Shaw
item.description: Sungrow has unveiled its third-generation commercial and industrial storage system, built around a modular expansion-dock architecture for multiple use cases.
item.content:encoded:
Sungrow launched the PowerStack 3.0 series, its latest commercial and industrial (C&I) energy storage platform, positioning the product as a shift from standardised physical integration toward what the company calls “scene-in-one” architecture designed to serve pure storage, solar-plus-storage, solar-storage-charging, and microgrid applications from a single hardware base.

The core of the launch is a “1+N=S” design — a standardised main cabinet paired with interchangeable expansion docks — which Sungrow describes as an industry-first approach to C&I storage. In the solar-plus-storage configuration, the company said a single power conversion system can absorb PV power conversion, eliminating the need for a separate PV inverter and supporting twice the rated PV capacity on the DC side. For the microgrid dock, Sungrow claims seamless grid-to-island transition without an external static transfer switch. These specific performance claims come from the manufacturer and have not been independently verified.

On the hardware side, PowerStack 3.0 uses 684 Ah laminated LFP cells, a full silicon carbide power conversion system rated at up to 99.2% peak efficiency, and a stated system round-trip efficiency of at least 92%. Energy density is listed at 256 kWh per square metre, which Sungrow said reduces footprint by 43% compared to conventional solutions. The system carries IP55 enclosure protection and C5 corrosion resistance, operates from −30 C to 50 C, and tolerates up to 30% grid harmonic content — specifications aimed at harsh industrial environments and weak-grid sites. Liquid cooling with AI-driven thermal management is said to cut auxiliary power consumption by 33% versus the previous generation.

The control architecture consolidates what Sungrow previously handled across four layers — energy management, cluster management, and local control — into a two-layer fusion controller. Each cabinet retains independent dispatch capability, with automatic host failover designed to keep the station running if a single unit drops offline. Units can be paralleled from one to 20 to scale from small commercial sites to campus-level installations.

Sungrow has also embedded an AI assistant, branded Bubbly, across the product lifecycle. The company claims the system can generate a site-specific design and revenue forecast in 30 seconds, complete complex scenario commissioning in three minutes, and lift operating revenue by 12% versus a self-consumption baseline through forecast-driven dispatch optimization. These figures are manufacturer projections based on internal modeling rather than field-validated results.

PowerStack 3.0 succeeds the company’s 255CS and 510CS C&I lines, and Sungrow said it is targeting Europe, Asia-Pacific, and the Middle East — regions where C&I storage demand is growing as electricity price volatility, demand-charge management, and behind-the-meter renewable integration drive more complex use cases. The underlying technology — large-format laminated cells, SiC conversion, and liquid cooling — has migrated from Sungrow’s utility-scale PowerTitan platform, reflecting a broader industry pattern of utility-grade hardware moving downstream into distributed applications.

From ESS News

item.title: Community opposition sends solar and storage project to IPC for review
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Metis Energy’s plans to build a 200 MW solar farm and 300 MWh battery in northern New South Wales are in the hands of the state’s Independent Planning Commission after the project attracted more than 100 qualifying objections.
item.content:encoded:
The Bendemeer Solar Farm and battery energy storage project, being developed Singapore-based Metis Energy through subsidiary Athena Energy, near Tamworth in the New South Wales (NSW) New England region, has been referred to the state’s Independent Planning Commission (IPC) for assessment.

The project, while deemed “approvable” by the NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure (DPHI), has been referred to the IPC as required under state planning laws after attracting 119 objections – 19 more than the new 100 threshold that triggers an assessment by the Commission.

The project, being developed near the township of Bendemeer, about 35 kilometres northeast of Tamworth, is to include a 200 MW solar farm and 150 MW / 300 MWh battery energy storage system. The solar and storage project is part of the proposed Bendemeer Renewable Energy Hub that could also include the development of a separately assessed 360 MW wind farm.

In its letter referring the Bendemeer solar and battery project, the NSW DPHI said it had visited the site, consulted with local residents, council and relevant government agencies, and had found the project “approvable subject to conditions.”

It is however now up to the IPC to make a call, based on the information provided by the department and any new information gathered through its own process.

The Bendemeer project, planned for a 369-hectare site that is currently used for sheep and cattle grazing, received 232 unique submissions during the public exhibition of its Environmental Impact Statement (EIS), including 109 that supported it, and four that provided comments. 

Key issues raised by those objecting to the project include site suitability, impacts on water quality and hydrology, biodiversity, and amenity. The submissions also raised concerns about the project’s impact on property values and on how benefits would be shared with community.

According to documents published by the NSW DPHI, the project has been progressively “designed and refined” by Athena to avoid and minimise negative impacts.

The Department said since first launching the project, Athena has reduced the development footprint by approximately 107 hectares, progressively refined the design to reduce native vegetation clearing, and developed a proposed conservation area within the site.

Athena has also reached an in-principle agreement with Tamworth Regional Council to enter into a Voluntary Planning Agreement, with a developer contribution of approximately $4.4 million.

In its referral documents, the NSW DPHI said the project would make a meaningful contribution to the state’s renewable energy transition and would not result in any significant impacts on the local community or the environment.

“Overall, the Department’s assessment concludes that the project would result in benefits to the state of NSW and considers the project is in the public interest,” it said,

The IPC will host a public meeting at the Bendemeer Town Hall on 5 December 2026 to help inform its decision, while written submissions will be accepted until 13 December 2026.
